newsitem.title: FRANCE: France taxes big business to meet euro goal.
newsitem.headline: France taxes big business to meet euro goal.

text.p: France's new left-wing government slapped a hefty surcharge on company profits on Monday to lower the budget deficit and bring the country into line for European monetary union.
The increase is meant to reconcile election campaign pledges to spare ordinary taxpayers new austerity and meet France's commitment to launching a single currency on time in 1999.
Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn, promising a fairer distribution of wealth, told a news conference the government would raise taxes on company profits and capital gains.

Altogther it planned measures to reduce the budget deficit, forecast by an audit of public finances released on Monday at 3.5 to 3.7 percent of gross domestic product, by 32 billion francs or 0.4 percentage points of GDP.
That would bring France within reach of the Maastricht treaty's three percent ceiling on budget deficits, but short of the 3.0 percent sought by its main ally, Germany.
"Less would have been insufficient, more would have blocked economic growth," Strauss-Kahn said. He also said the 1998 budget would limit the deficit to three percent.
France's European partners, edgy about Paris' commitment to monetary union since the left's surprise parliamentary election victory on June 1, welcomed the announcement.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel, who spoke with Strauss-Kahn by telephone before the announcement, said Paris wanted to meet the Maastricht deficit goal in 1997 and 1998.
He declined to speculate on France's chances of meeting those goals, but said "it is certain that monetary union without France or Germany makes little sense."
Luxembourg Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker, whose country holds the EU presidency, said "the French decision clearly shows France is committed to EMU and committed to the start date."

Private economists, while welcoming the commitment to economic and monetary union, said that attacking the corporate sector could undermine business confidence and threaten a long-awaited pick-up in investment.

"It will have a negative impact on business confidence at exactly the wrong time," UBS economist Darren Williams said, adding that companies were already worried about the government's plans to reduce the working week to boost jobs.
"They are taking a risk with the recovery," he said.
Some also bewailed the lack of structural reforms which France's European partners say are needed to bring down unemployment and free up the economy.
"They cannot keep using these cosmetic measures to cut the deficit. They must undertake fundamental reforms," Deutsche Bank economist Patrick Mange said.

That call was also made by the auditors themselves, who said in their independent report that France, where the state still plays a big role, must improve the efficiency of state intervention to make a lasting improvement in public finances.
Growth alone would not be enough to cut the deficit. "Deep-rooted reforms are lacking as regards the state," auditors Philippe Nasse and Jacques Bonnet said.
"French public finances are in crisis," they wrote. "It is high time to undertake these reforms. It is more than time."
In line with Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's campaign pledge that there would be "no new austerity" to qualify for EMU, the package contained no tax increase on households.

Strauss-Kahn said the 32 billion franc deficit reduction package would include 10 billion in savings, including two billion from the defence budget, with the rest coming from the company tax increases.
Arguing that company profits were at a record high, he announced a 15 percent surcharge on company tax in 1997 and 1998 falling to 10 percent in 1999.
The increase is calculated on the 33.3 percent basic rate, and comes on top of a 10 percent surcharge introduced in 1995 which took the effective tax rate to 36.6 percent.
The new effective tax rate will be 41.6 percent falling to 39.9 percent in 1999. Small firms were exempted from the rise.
Corporate capital gains, taxed previously at 19 percent, will now be taxed at the same rate as profits, although this will not apply to share sales, the finance ministry said.

French markets showed little reaction to the announcements which had been widely leaked in advance. The CAC-40 blue-chip index finished down 0.09 percent. Bonds were steady and the franc ended slightly higher against the mark.
The centre-right opposition attacked the government.

"The economic choices of the government go against the liberal policies which, throughout the world, allow growth and employment, via cuts in state spending, lower taxes and privatisations," said Alain Madelin, leader of the right-wing Liberal Democracy party. "You can't be part of the euro game by swimming against the European tide," he said.
